8.2 — Boss Body, Health & Phases

Your spec exists on paper (8.1). Today it becomes an object standing in a room. But there is nothing to drag in: this project has no boss prefab, and if you search Assets/Prefabs for one you will come up empty. You are about to assemble a boss out of the enemy art that is already here, give it a shape the physics engine can find, give it a number that says how alive it is, and make that number change its mind at two thresholds. Health first, attacks in 8.4 — a boss you cannot hurt is a boss you cannot tune.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I build a boss when there is no boss prefab?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

A boss that stands in a room, can be hit, and changes its mind twice as its health falls — in a project that contains no boss at all. As one problem it is not startable, because there is nothing to drag in: the body, its shape, its number, where that number is kept and the rules on it all have to be decided before any of them can be written.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Assemble the body out of art that is already herewhat does this part do?Read: 8.1 — Boss Design: Spec It First: the honest inventory of what this project ships, and the scene you chose to host the fight
  2. Give the body a shape the physics engine can findwhat does this part do?Read: 2.1 — Coins: Triggers, Tags & Your First Stat: the collider you added to the coin, the body you added to the Player, and the renderer-on-a-child discovery
  3. Give the body a number, and one method that can subtract from itwhat does this part do?Read: 2.2 — Spikes: Physics, Damage & Death: the signed damage method, and 2.3 — Healing Pickups & the Max-Health Cap: the rule that bounds a value inside the method that changes it
  4. Decide where that number lives — and it is the opposite answer to the player'swhat does this part do?Read: 5.3 — Into the Cave: Scenes, Persistence & The Refactor: StatManager.Instance, the Awake() that claims it, DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject) and the duplicate guard
  5. Guard each threshold so it fires once, on a crossingwhat does this part do?Read: 3.3 — Fire Rate: Cooldowns & Time: a rule that fires once and must then wait — and the phase table you wrote in 8.1
  6. Make the change visible before any attack existswhat does this part do?Read: the Debug.Log readout you have watched since 2.1, against the HUD you built in 5.3

The split follows one number through its whole life: an object is assembled, given a shape, given a value, told where to keep that value, given rules about when it may change, and finally made visible. Four of those six parts are things you have already built — a collider, a signed damage method, a persistence decision and a rule that fires once. What is new is small enough to miss: none of it is boss code. This is the coin, the spike, the singleton and the cooldown, pointed at one object and told to hold still.

The test for a finished split: does the part name something you could point at — a component, an object in the Hierarchy, a field, a method, a scene? "Build a boss" points at nothing. "Which object carries the collider the player will hit" points at one object in one hierarchy, and that is a part.

Your turn

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

Your player's health and your boss's health are both numbers that go down. Say which of the two lives on an object a scene load cannot delete, and what the player would find in the arena if you gave the boss the same answer you gave the player.

A threshold is a boundary, not a value. Say in one line what your guard actually checks — the crossing, or the current health — and describe what the fight looks like on the day the other one ships.

The Problem: Assembling Something From Parts That Are Not It ~10 min

Open Assets/Artwork/Character/Enemy/. You will find four assets: OrcwithAxe1.png, OrcwithAxe2.png, a LoRTowerV2_blue_no_soul_no_fire-Sheet.png (a tower — the same family as your turret), and Turret_Bullet.png. There is no boss sheet, and there is never going to be one. A boss in a small project is assembled, not delivered: it is existing art, scaled, recombined, and re-contextualised until it reads as something the player has not seen before.

That is a real design skill and it is the one this lesson teaches. Before you choose, read the three honest options and what each one costs:

ApproachWhat you doWhat it costsWhen it wins
(a) Scale an existing enemy up Take Assets/Prefabs/MobileEnemy — the prefab is named MobileEnemy — duplicate it, rename the copy, and scale it to roughly three times size. Or rebuild the same thing as a fresh GameObject with an orc sprite from the Enemy folder. Scaling up also scales every collider under it, and reveals every soft edge in the art. Check the hierarchy before you pick a number, too: the enemy's Sprite child is already at 1.5× on its own transform, so 3× on the root is nearer 4.5× the art. And it reads as "the same enemy, bigger" unless you change something else about it. You want a boss that moves like your enemies already do and can reuse their animation setup unchanged.
(b) Make the environment the boss Build the boss out of the LoRTowerV2 tower sheet — a fixed emplacement that does not chase you, only fires. It cannot charge or reposition, so any spec attack that involves movement has to be rewritten as a projectile or a hazard. Your spec (8.1) is built around ranged pressure and an arena you must cross.
(c) Recombine: a scaled body plus a child emplacement An orc scaled up, with a scaled-down tower sprite as a child — a rider, a shoulder cannon, a crown. Two pieces the player has seen separately, in a combination they have not. Two things to keep aligned, and the child will fire from an offset you have to tune. Your spec has at least one attack that does not come from the body — which is most interesting bosses.
You do not get to skip the Inspector read. Select your chosen source object and list every component it carries. Then list what is missing for a boss: a shape the physics engine can find, a script that owns its health, and a decision about which object the player's swing will actually hit in 8.3. In 2.1 you discovered that the objects you are handed arrive with no collider and no body at all — the coin, the Player, the enemy and the turret are all shapes with a picture on them and nothing the physics engine can find — which is why you added the coin's collider and the Player's body yourself. Nothing you assemble for this boss will arrive with one either.

Socratic: What Is a Boss Made Of?

  1. You scaled an enemy to three times its size. Which two things scaled with it that you did not intend to change — one in the scene, one in how the fight feels?
  2. Your player is a small character in a room. If the boss's collider is enormous, what happens to the player's ability to walk past it — and does your spec's arena still work?
  3. A boss made of two recombined pieces gives you a second place attacks can come from. Which attack in your 8.1 spec could come from a child object rather than the body?
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

Phase thresholds are guards: a rule that fires once, at a boundary, and never again. Here are five guards from other worlds. None of them is game code — read each one and ask what the equivalent boundary is in your boss.

Example 1 — A railway signal box (the guard is the safety system):

// A lever moves the points only if the signal is not already clear.
// The guard is not a formality - it is the whole safety system.

Example 2 — Stadium floodlights at halftime (once per match, not once per reading):

// The halftime cue fires once. Without the guard, every dimmer
// reading below 50% would re-run the entire sequence.

Example 3 — A factory quality gate (two thresholds, two responses):

// The line inspector flags a batch at a 50% reject rate
// and stops the line at 20%. Same sensor, two different rules.

Example 4 — A vending machine's exact-change light (a boundary, not a value):

// "Exact change only" comes on at the moment the coin box
// crosses the line. It does not re-announce for every coin after.

Example 5 — The stadium scoreboard (bolted to the stadium, not to the team):

// The scoreboard does not travel with the team. Whatever shows
// a score has to live where the score is being kept.

Predict Before Building

  1. In the floodlight example, what exactly is the guard — the cue, or the state that says the cue has already run? Which one will you need in your boss script?
  2. The quality gate fires two different responses from one sensor. In your spec, what are the two responses at your two thresholds — and are they different enough to be worth two thresholds instead of one?
  3. The scoreboard example is about where a number lives. Your player's health lives in a singleton that survives scene loads. If the boss's health lived there too, what would happen to the boss's health when the player walked out of the arena and back in?
Build Lab: The Body, the Collider, the Number ~30 min

Step 1 — place the body. Build your boss in the scene you named in 8.1. Settle one thing first: your player's stats live in an object that survives scene loads, but the boss's health must not — a boss that carried its wounds across a scene change would be a very strange boss. So where does the boss's health live, and why is that the opposite answer to the one you gave in 5.3? Name the object Boss so you can find it in the Hierarchy at a glance.

Step 2 — give it a shape. Read the Inspector of your source object and work out which object in your boss's hierarchy carries the SpriteRenderer. In 2.1 you learned that the coin's renderer is on a child and that a default collider on the root therefore does not necessarily cover what you can see. Check it. Then press Play and walk into your boss — does it stop you, or do you stroll through it, and which of those two results does your spec need?

Step 3 — give it a number. The boss needs its own health, and something has to be able to subtract from it. Write the smallest version of that: a maximum, a current value, and one method that takes a signed amount — the same shape as the damage method you built on the player in Unit 2 and then moved into StatManager in 5.3. Print the new value with Debug.Log so you can watch it fall without building any UI for it — the HUD you built in 5.3 reads the player's stats, not the boss's — and it is the same instrument you watched for coins in 2.1.

Architectural specification: where does the boss's health live?
  • Your player's health lives in StatManager, which is a singleton with DontDestroyOnLoad — a decision you made in 5.3 for a specific reason. What was that reason, and does it apply to a boss?
  • If you stored the boss's remaining health in the same singleton, what would the player find when they died, reloaded, and walked back into the arena? Trace it through step by step.
  • The boss lives in one scene. Name the property of the boss's lifetime that decides where its numbers belong — and say whether that property is the same as the player's.
  • Would you put the boss's health on a component of its own, or on the same script that will later schedule its attacks in 8.4? Argue the split point, then write it that way.
  • Which object is the player's swing actually going to hit in 8.3 — the collider on the body you just made, or a separate one? Whichever you choose, what has to be true about it for a query to find it?
Architectural specification: the phase thresholds.
  • How many thresholds does your spec have, at what values, and what is the response at each one?
  • A threshold check that reads "health is below X" fires on every frame the boss is below X. A guard that reads "the boss is not already in this phase" fires once. Which do you need, and what does the other one do to your fight?
  • Phase changes only ever move forward, and only downward through the health values. Why is a phase transition that can run backwards a bug generator rather than a feature?
  • What if two thresholds are crossed in a single hit? Which phase should the boss be in afterwards, and what does that tell you about the order of your checks?
  • What is the smallest visible effect you can give a phase change today, before any attacks exist? Name the one the player will actually notice within a second.
Read which properties the clips animate before you blame the Animator. An Animator overwrites exactly the properties its clips carry keys for, every frame, and touches nothing else. So the question is never "does my boss have an Animator" — every enemy here does — it is "what do those clips write". You can answer it without pressing Play: open one clip from Assets/Artwork/Animations/Top_Down/EnemyMotion/ in the Animation window and read the property list. Every clip in that folder animates the sprite and nothing else — there are no position keys and no scale keys anywhere in the set — so a 3× scale you set on a body those clips drive survives Play. A controller you build yourself whose telegraph is a scale punch is the other answer: there the clip wins and your Inspector edit vanishes without an error. Know which of the two you have, and scale a parent if you are ever unsure.
Read the Docs: Two Decisions With More Than One Right Answer ~15 min

Read both tables, pick a row from each, and be ready to defend it. Neither has a single correct answer — but each has a cost you are accepting.

Health displayWhat it looks likeWhat it costsWhen it wins
(a) Debug.Log Every health change prints the new value. Only you can see it. It is not a game, it is an instrument. Today. It is the instrument you have watched all year, and it costs nothing to build. It is also the correct instrument for a boss: 5.3's HUD exists to show the player's own stats, and the boss is not the player.
(b) A world-space bar Three child sprites — a background, a fill, and a frame — with the fill's localScale.x driven by the health fraction. No Canvas involved. You must handle the fraction reaching zero without inverting the sprite, and it scales with the boss. You want the player to watch the bar fall, and you are not ready to take on a whole UI system yet.
(c) A UI Slider on a Canvas The conventional answer: a Canvas, a Slider anchored to the top of the screen, and a reference from the boss. You already met a Canvas in 5.3 — but that one is a line of text showing your stats, and it lives in Start. A boss bar is a second screen-space problem: a new RectTransform hierarchy anchored to a corner, and a decision about which scene it belongs to — 5.3's Canvas is in Start, and your arena lives in whichever scene you named in 8.1. The subsystem is familiar; the anchoring work is not. You want the standard look, and you are ready to find out how much of 5.3's HUD you can reuse for something that is not the player's.
Animating the bossWhat it looks likeWhat it costsWhen it wins
(a) Reuse the enemy controller Drive MobileEnemy's existing Animator Controller: a Direction integer (0 = Right, 1 = Up, 2 = Left, 3 = Down) and an Attack trigger, with separate Walk and Attack states per direction. That controller has no idle states — so a boss standing still still looks like it is walking. And it uses a separate clip per horizontal direction rather than flipping the sprite, so you cannot mirror it cheaply. Your boss moves like your existing enemies do, and you want the animations working today.
(b) Build a new Animator Controller Two states — Idle and Attack — reusing the same clips in a controller you own. You must learn the Animator window's transition graph properly, and you inherit every mistake in the original clips. Your spec is built around standing still and telegraphing, and the walk states would be noise.
(c) No Animator at all A static sprite whose telegraph is a scale punch or a colour flash driven from your own script. Almost no expressive range — but a colour flash is a genuinely good telegraph, and it is the cheapest one to build. You want the fight working first and the animation second, which is the correct order for a deadline.

Choose, Then Justify

  1. Which health display did you choose, and which row of the table did you reject? What is the cost you accepted?
  2. The world-space bar drives localScale.x from a fraction. What does that fraction look like on the frame the boss dies, and what would the bar do if you forgot to clamp it?
  3. The reusable enemy controller has no idle states. What does the player conclude about a boss that appears to be walking while standing still — and is that a bug you can live with, or one you must fix?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain why the boss had to be assembled rather than found, and name the art you assembled it from
  • State which object in your boss carries the renderer, and which object carries the collider the player will hit
  • Explain why the boss's health is scene-local while the player's health is a singleton — in terms of lifetime, not tidiness
  • Explain why a phase threshold must be guarded, and what happens without the guard
  • Defend your choice of health display and animation approach, naming what each one cost
  • Break this feature into parts small enough to look each one up on its own, and say in one line what each part does
  • Say which earlier lesson each part of this feature came from, and where you would reread it
  • Commit and push
